brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome is a very rare genetic disorder which is characterized by symmetric brachydactyly of the fingers accompanied by an abnormally long thumb, hypomobility of the shoulder and metacarpo-phalangeal joints, and heart conduction defects. small feet and hands, small shoulders accompanied with short clavicles, clinodactyly, pectus excavatum, mild limb shortening, cardiomegaly, and pulmonic stenosis murmur have also been reported.[1][2] it was first discovered when d w hollister et al. described 4 affected members belonging to a 3-generation family.[3][4][5] no new cases have been reported since 1981.[6] this disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.[7]

section: introduction
brachydactyly (from greek  βραχύς (brachus) 'short' and  δάκτυλος (daktulos) 'finger') is a medical term denoting the presence of abnormally short digits (fingers or toes) at birth. the shortness is relative to the length of other long bones and other parts of the body. brachydactyly is an inherited, dominant trait. it most often occurs as an isolated dysmelia, but can also occur with other anomalies as part of many congenital syndromes. brachydactyly may also be a signal that one is at risk for congenital heart disease[1] due to the association between congenital heart disease and carpenter syndrome and the link between carpenter syndrome and brachydactyly.[2] nomograms for normal values of finger length as a ratio to other body measurements have been published. in clinical genetics, the most commonly used index of digit length is the dimensionless ratio of the length of the third (middle) finger to the hand length. both are expressed in the same units (centimeters, for example) and are measured in an open hand from the fingertip to the principal creases where the finger joins the palm and where the palm joins the wrist.
section: symptoms
symptoms of isolated brachydactyly include shorter bones in the hands and feet. this could include, phalanges, metacarpals, metatarsals, carpals, and tarsals. different types of isolated brachydactyly have different symptoms and they are grouped according to what areas they affect.
section: prognosis
isolated brachydactyly does not affect the wellbeing nor longevity of one's life, in most cases treatment is not necessary.[4] the trait is primarily a cosmetic one and does not, in most cases, affect function of the hands and feet. even left untreated and affecting function the general diagnosis of brachydactyly does not impact life expectancy. prognosis may differ with different types or syndromes. ie. brachydactyly-mesomelia-intellectual disability-heart defects syndrome or if brachydactyly is not isolated and is a part of a larger genetic condition. in rare cases of isolated untreated brachydactyly, simple functions like walking or grabbing objects may be difficult, reducing the overall quality of life.

section: other syndromes
in the above brachydactyly syndromes, short digits are the most prominent of the anomalies, but in many other syndromes (down syndrome, rubinstein–taybi syndrome, etc.), brachydactyly is a minor feature compared to the other anomalies or problems comprising the syndrome.

- reference: [crawl_ner_wiki_2] - information about: brachydactyly type d - brachydactyly
section: introduction
brachydactyly type d, also known as murderer's thumb,[3][1] stubbed thumb,[4][5] spoon thumb, power thumb or short thumb,[4][5] is a genetic trait recognised by a thumb being relatively short and round with an accompanying wider nail bed. the distal phalanx of such thumbs is approximately two-thirds the length of full-length thumbs. it is the most common type of shortness of digits (brachydactyly), affecting approximately 2% of the population. it is associated with the hoxd13 gene, located on chromosome 2q31.1.[6]
section: signs and symptoms
brachydactyly type d is a skeletal condition that exhibits a “partial fusion or premature closing of the epiphysis with the distal phalanx of the thumb,” according to goodman et alia (1965).[5] j.k. breitenbecher (1923) found that the distal phalanges of short thumbs were one-half the length of full-length thumbs, while r.m. stecher (1957) claimed that it is approximately two-thirds. the condition may be unilateral (affecting one thumb) or bilateral (affecting both).[5]
section: genetics
brachydactyly type d is a genetic trait. it exhibits autosomal dominance and is commonly developed or inherited independently of other hereditary traits. the condition is associated with the hoxd13 gene, which is central in digital formation and growth.[4] various other studies supported an autosomal dominant pattern with reduced penetrance.[7][8]
section: terminology
the condition is also called clubbed thumb or club thumb.[9][10] american researcher r.a. hefner used the terms "short thumb" and "brachymegalodactylism" in 1924,[3] and "short thumb" has continued to be used in a few other studies since then, including the study that defined rubinstein–taybi syndrome in 1963.[1] "stub thumb" is the common term preferred by the online database online mendelian inheritance in man[4] and was first used in a 1965 study.[5] stub thumbs have also been called hammer thumbs, bohemian thumbs, and potter's thumbs.[4]

Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly (from Greek  βραχύς (brachus) 'short' and  δάκτυλος (daktulos) 'finger') is a medical term denoting the presence of abnormally short digits (fingers or toes) at birth. The shortness is relative to the length of other long bones and other parts of the body. Brachydactyly is an inherited, dominant trait. It most often occurs as an isolated dysmelia, but can also occur with other anomalies as part of many congenital syndromes. Brachydactyly may also be a signal that one is at risk for congenital heart disease[1] due to the association between congenital heart disease and Carpenter syndrome and the link between Carpenter syndrome and brachydactyly.[2] Nomograms for normal values of finger length as a ratio to other body measurements have been published. In clinical genetics, the most commonly used index of digit length is the dimensionless ratio of the length of the third (middle) finger to the hand length. Both are expressed in the same units (centimeters, for example) and are measured in an open hand from the fingertip to the principal creases where the finger joins the palm and where the palm joins the wrist.
Section: Symptoms
Symptoms of isolated brachydactyly include shorter bones in the hands and feet. This could include, phalanges, metacarpals, metatarsals, carpals, and tarsals. Different types of isolated brachydactyly have different symptoms and they are grouped according to what areas they affect.
Section: Prognosis
Isolated brachydactyly does not affect the wellbeing nor longevity of one's life, in most cases treatment is not necessary.[4] The trait is primarily a cosmetic one and does not, in most cases, affect function of the hands and feet. Even left untreated and affecting function the general diagnosis of brachydactyly does not impact life expectancy. Prognosis may differ with different types or syndromes. ie. brachydactyly-mesomelia-intellectual disability-heart defects syndrome or if brachydactyly is not isolated and is a part of a larger genetic condition. In rare cases of isolated untreated brachydactyly, simple functions like walking or grabbing objects may be difficult, reducing the overall quality of life.

Brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome is a very rare genetic disorder which is characterized by symmetric brachydactyly of the fingers accompanied by an abnormally long thumb, hypomobility of the shoulder and metacarpo-phalangeal joints, and heart conduction defects. - Reference: [CRAWL_WIKI_1] - Information about: Brachydactyly
Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly (from Greek  βραχύς (brachus) 'short' and  δάκτυλος (daktulos) 'finger') is a medical term denoting the presence of abnormally short digits (fingers or toes) at birth. The shortness is relative to the length of other long bones and other parts of the body. Brachydactyly is an inherited, dominant trait. It most often occurs as an isolated dysmelia, but can also occur with other anomalies as part of many congenital syndromes. Brachydactyly may also be a signal that one is at risk for congenital heart disease[1] due to the association between congenital heart disease and Carpenter syndrome and the link between Carpenter syndrome and brachydactyly.[2] Nomograms for normal values of finger length as a ratio to other body measurements have been published. In clinical genetics, the most commonly used index of digit length is the dimensionless ratio of the length of the third (middle) finger to the hand length. Both are expressed in the same units (centimeters, for example) and are measured in an open hand from the fingertip to the principal creases where the finger joins the palm and where the palm joins the wrist.
Section: Symptoms
Symptoms of isolated brachydactyly include shorter bones in the hands and feet. This could include, phalanges, metacarpals, metatarsals, carpals, and tarsals. Different types of isolated brachydactyly have different symptoms and they are grouped according to what areas they affect.
Section: Prognosis
Isolated brachydactyly does not affect the wellbeing nor longevity of one's life, in most cases treatment is not necessary.[4] The trait is primarily a cosmetic one and does not, in most cases, affect function of the hands and feet. Even left untreated and affecting function the general diagnosis of brachydactyly does not impact life expectancy. Prognosis may differ with different types or syndromes. ie. brachydactyly-mesomelia-intellectual disability-heart defects syndrome or if brachydactyly is not isolated and is a part of a larger genetic condition. In rare cases of isolated untreated brachydactyly, simple functions like walking or grabbing objects may be difficult, reducing the overall quality of life.
Section: Types
There are several types of brachydactyly:
Section: Other syndromes
In the above brachydactyly syndromes, short digits are the most prominent of the anomalies, but in many other syndromes (Down syndrome, Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome, etc.), brachydactyly is a minor feature compared to the other anomalies or problems comprising the syndrome.

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_2] - Information about: Brachydactyly type D - brachydactyly
Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly type D, also known as murderer's thumb,[3][1] stubbed thumb,[4][5] spoon thumb, power thumb or short thumb,[4][5] is a genetic trait recognised by a thumb being relatively short and round with an accompanying wider nail bed. The distal phalanx of such thumbs is approximately two-thirds the length of full-length thumbs. It is the most common type of shortness of digits (brachydactyly), affecting approximately 2% of the population. It is associated with the HOXD13 gene, located on chromosome 2q31.1.[6]
Section: Signs and symptoms
Brachydactyly type D is a skeletal condition that exhibits a “partial fusion or premature closing of the epiphysis with the distal phalanx of the thumb,” according to Goodman et alia (1965).[5] J.K. Breitenbecher (1923) found that the distal phalanges of short thumbs were one-half the length of full-length thumbs, while R.M. Stecher (1957) claimed that it is approximately two-thirds. The condition may be unilateral (affecting one thumb) or bilateral (affecting both).[5]
Section: Genetics
Brachydactyly type D is a genetic trait. It exhibits autosomal dominance and is commonly developed or inherited independently of other hereditary traits. The condition is associated with the HOXD13 gene, which is central in digital formation and growth.[4] Various other studies supported an autosomal dominant pattern with reduced penetrance.[7][8]
Section: Terminology
The condition is also called clubbed thumb or club thumb.[9][10] American researcher R.A. Hefner used the terms "short thumb" and "brachymegalodactylism" in 1924,[3] and "short thumb" has continued to be used in a few other studies since then, including the study that defined Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome in 1963.[1] "Stub thumb" is the common term preferred by the online database Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man[4] and was first used in a 1965 study.[5] Stub thumbs have also been called hammer thumbs, bohemian thumbs, and potter's thumbs.[4]

llm.short_answer: Carpenter syndrome is a congenital condition with craniofacial and limb anomalies including brachydactyly and syndactyly.
llm.long_answer: Reference: [GG_5], [GG_19], [GG_20]. Detailed explanation: Carpenter syndrome, also known as acrocephalopolysyndactyly, is a congenital disorder characterized by abnormalities in craniofacial development and limb formation. Its associated symptoms include brachydactyly, which is the presence of unusually short fingers or toes, and syndactyly, where these digits may be fused or webbed.

llm.short_answer: Carpenter syndrome is a congenital malformation disorder marked by craniosynostosis, brachydactyly, polysyndactyly, and other developmental anomalies such as congenital heart defects.
llm.long_answer: Reference: [GG_9], [GG_10], [GG_14], [GG_15]. Detailed explanation: Carpenter syndrome is described as a multiple congenital malformation disorder. It is characterized by the premature fusion of skull bones (craniosynostosis) and abnormalities affecting the hands and feet, such as brachydactyly (short digits) and polysyndactyly (extra or fused digits). Additionally, some cases may present with congenital heart defects and other developmental anomalies. One referenced form, Carpenter syndrome-2, is noted to be inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.

Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome is a very rare genetic disorder which is characterized by symmetric brachydactyly of the fingers accompanied by an abnormally long thumb, hypomobility of the shoulder and metacarpo-phalangeal joints, and heart conduction defects. Small feet and hands, small shoulders accompanied with short clavicles, clinodactyly, pectus excavatum, mild limb shortening, cardiomegaly, and pulmonic stenosis murmur have also been reported.[1][2] It was first discovered when D W Hollister et al. described 4 affected members belonging to a 3-generation family.[3][4][5] No new cases have been reported since 1981.[6] This disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.[7]

- Reference: [CRAWL_WIKI_1] - Information about: Brachydactyly
Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly (from Greek  βραχύς (brachus) 'short' and  δάκτυλος (daktulos) 'finger') is a medical term denoting the presence of abnormally short digits (fingers or toes) at birth. The shortness is relative to the length of other long bones and other parts of the body. Brachydactyly is an inherited, dominant trait. It most often occurs as an isolated dysmelia, but can also occur with other anomalies as part of many congenital syndromes. Brachydactyly may also be a signal that one is at risk for congenital heart disease[1] due to the association between congenital heart disease and Carpenter syndrome and the link between Carpenter syndrome and brachydactyly.[2] Nomograms for normal values of finger length as a ratio to other body measurements have been published. In clinical genetics, the most commonly used index of digit length is the dimensionless ratio of the length of the third (middle) finger to the hand length. Both are expressed in the same units (centimeters, for example) and are measured in an open hand from the fingertip to the principal creases where the finger joins the palm and where the palm joins the wrist.
Section: Symptoms
Symptoms of isolated brachydactyly include shorter bones in the hands and feet. This could include, phalanges, metacarpals, metatarsals, carpals, and tarsals. Different types of isolated brachydactyly have different symptoms and they are grouped according to what areas they affect.
Section: Prognosis
Isolated brachydactyly does not affect the wellbeing nor longevity of one's life, in most cases treatment is not necessary.[4] The trait is primarily a cosmetic one and does not, in most cases, affect function of the hands and feet. Even left untreated and affecting function the general diagnosis of brachydactyly does not impact life expectancy. Prognosis may differ with different types or syndromes. ie. brachydactyly-mesomelia-intellectual disability-heart defects syndrome or if brachydactyly is not isolated and is a part of a larger genetic condition. In rare cases of isolated untreated brachydactyly, simple functions like walking or grabbing objects may be difficult, reducing the overall quality of life.

Section: Other syndromes
In the above brachydactyly syndromes, short digits are the most prominent of the anomalies, but in many other syndromes (Down syndrome, Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome, etc.), brachydactyly is a minor feature compared to the other anomalies or problems comprising the syndrome.

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_2] - Information about: Brachydactyly type D - brachydactyly
Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly type D, also known as murderer's thumb,[3][1] stubbed thumb,[4][5] spoon thumb, power thumb or short thumb,[4][5] is a genetic trait recognised by a thumb being relatively short and round with an accompanying wider nail bed. The distal phalanx of such thumbs is approximately two-thirds the length of full-length thumbs. It is the most common type of shortness of digits (brachydactyly), affecting approximately 2% of the population. It is associated with the HOXD13 gene, located on chromosome 2q31.1.[6]
Section: Signs and symptoms
Brachydactyly type D is a skeletal condition that exhibits a “partial fusion or premature closing of the epiphysis with the distal phalanx of the thumb,” according to Goodman et alia (1965).[5] J.K. Breitenbecher (1923) found that the distal phalanges of short thumbs were one-half the length of full-length thumbs, while R.M. Stecher (1957) claimed that it is approximately two-thirds. The condition may be unilateral (affecting one thumb) or bilateral (affecting both).[5]
Section: Genetics
Brachydactyly type D is a genetic trait. It exhibits autosomal dominance and is commonly developed or inherited independently of other hereditary traits. The condition is associated with the HOXD13 gene, which is central in digital formation and growth.[4] Various other studies supported an autosomal dominant pattern with reduced penetrance.[7][8]
Section: Terminology
The condition is also called clubbed thumb or club thumb.[9][10] American researcher R.A. Hefner used the terms "short thumb" and "brachymegalodactylism" in 1924,[3] and "short thumb" has continued to be used in a few other studies since then, including the study that defined Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome in 1963.[1] "Stub thumb" is the common term preferred by the online database Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man[4] and was first used in a 1965 study.[5] Stub thumbs have also been called hammer thumbs, bohemian thumbs, and potter's thumbs.[4]

llm.long_answer: Reference: [GG_13]. Detailed explanation: According to reference [GG_13], Carpenter syndrome (CS) is defined as a condition in which patients exhibit varying degrees of craniosynostosis (premature fusion of skull bones) along with brachydactyly (abnormally short digits), syndactyly (fusion of the fingers and toes), and polysyndactyly (extra digits in combination with syndactyly). These symptoms together form the clinical picture of Carpenter syndrome.

Brachydactyly (from Greek  βραχύς (brachus) 'short' and  δάκτυλος (daktulos) 'finger') is a medical term denoting the presence of abnormally short digits (fingers or toes) at birth. The shortness is relative to the length of other long bones and other parts of the body. Brachydactyly is an inherited, dominant trait. It most often occurs as an isolated dysmelia, but can also occur with other anomalies as part of many congenital syndromes. Brachydactyly may also be a signal that one is at risk for congenital heart disease[1] due to the association between congenital heart disease and Carpenter syndrome and the link between Carpenter syndrome and brachydactyly.[2] Nomograms for normal values of finger length as a ratio to other body measurements have been published. In clinical genetics, the most commonly used index of digit length is the dimensionless ratio of the length of the third (middle) finger to the hand length. Both are expressed in the same units (centimeters, for example) and are measured in an open hand from the fingertip to the principal creases where the finger joins the palm and where the palm joins the wrist.
Section: Symptoms
Symptoms of isolated brachydactyly include shorter bones in the hands and feet. This could include, phalanges, metacarpals, metatarsals, carpals, and tarsals. Different types of isolated brachydactyly have different symptoms and they are grouped according to what areas they affect.
Section: Prognosis
Isolated brachydactyly does not affect the wellbeing nor longevity of one's life, in most cases treatment is not necessary.[4] The trait is primarily a cosmetic one and does not, in most cases, affect function of the hands and feet. Even left untreated and affecting function the general diagnosis of brachydactyly does not impact life expectancy. Prognosis may differ with different types or syndromes. ie. brachydactyly-mesomelia-intellectual disability-heart defects syndrome or if brachydactyly is not isolated and is a part of a larger genetic condition. In rare cases of isolated untreated brachydactyly, simple functions like walking or grabbing objects may be difficult, reducing the overall quality of life.

Section: Other syndromes
In the above brachydactyly syndromes, short digits are the most prominent of the anomalies, but in many other syndromes (Down syndrome, Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome, etc.), brachydactyly is a minor feature compared to the other anomalies or problems comprising the syndrome.

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_2] - Information about: Brachydactyly type D - brachydactyly
Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly type D, also known as murderer's thumb,[3][1] stubbed thumb,[4][5] spoon thumb, power thumb or short thumb,[4][5] is a genetic trait recognised by a thumb being relatively short and round with an accompanying wider nail bed. The distal phalanx of such thumbs is approximately two-thirds the length of full-length thumbs. It is the most common type of shortness of digits (brachydactyly), affecting approximately 2% of the population. It is associated with the HOXD13 gene, located on chromosome 2q31.1.[6]
Section: Signs and symptoms
Brachydactyly type D is a skeletal condition that exhibits a “partial fusion or premature closing of the epiphysis with the distal phalanx of the thumb,” according to Goodman et alia (1965).[5] J.K. Breitenbecher (1923) found that the distal phalanges of short thumbs were one-half the length of full-length thumbs, while R.M. Stecher (1957) claimed that it is approximately two-thirds. The condition may be unilateral (affecting one thumb) or bilateral (affecting both).[5]
Section: Genetics
Brachydactyly type D is a genetic trait. It exhibits autosomal dominance and is commonly developed or inherited independently of other hereditary traits. The condition is associated with the HOXD13 gene, which is central in digital formation and growth.[4] Various other studies supported an autosomal dominant pattern with reduced penetrance.[7][8]
Section: Terminology
The condition is also called clubbed thumb or club thumb.[9][10] American researcher R.A. Hefner used the terms "short thumb" and "brachymegalodactylism" in 1924,[3] and "short thumb" has continued to be used in a few other studies since then, including the study that defined Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome in 1963.[1] "Stub thumb" is the common term preferred by the online database Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man[4] and was first used in a 1965 study.[5] Stub thumbs have also been called hammer thumbs, bohemian thumbs, and potter's thumbs.[4]

llm.short_answer: Carpenter syndrome is a congenital disorder characterized by brachydactyly with syndactyly of the hands, along with preaxial polydactyly and syndactyly of the feet, congenital heart defects, and growth retardation.
llm.long_answer: Reference: [GG_18]. Detailed explanation: According to the provided context, Carpenter syndrome (specifically Carpenter syndrome 1; CRPT1) is a condition that presents with brachydactyly of the hands accompanied by syndactyly, as well as preaxial polydactyly and syndactyly of the feet. Additional associated symptoms include congenital heart defects, growth retardation, and other impairments. This cluster of features defines Carpenter syndrome as a multisystem congenital disorder with limb anomalies and systemic implications.

Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome is a very rare genetic disorder which is characterized by symmetric brachydactyly of the fingers accompanied by an abnormally long thumb, hypomobility of the shoulder and metacarpo-phalangeal joints, and heart conduction defects. Small feet and hands, small shoulders accompanied with short clavicles, clinodactyly, pectus excavatum, mild limb shortening, cardiomegaly, and pulmonic stenosis murmur have also been reported.[1][2] It was first discovered when D W Hollister et al. described 4 affected members belonging to a 3-generation family.[3][4][5] No new cases have been reported since 1981.[6] This disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.[7]

Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly type D, also known as murderer's thumb,[3][1] stubbed thumb,[4][5] spoon thumb, power thumb or short thumb,[4][5] is a genetic trait recognised by a thumb being relatively short and round with an accompanying wider nail bed. Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly (from Greek  βραχύς (brachus) 'short' and  δάκτυλος (daktulos) 'finger') is a medical term denoting the presence of abnormally short digits (fingers or toes) at birth. It most often occurs as an isolated dysmelia, but can also occur with other anomalies as part of many congenital syndromes. In clinical genetics, the most commonly used index of digit length is the dimensionless ratio of the length of the third (middle) finger to the hand length. Both are expressed in the same units (centimeters, for example) and are measured in an open hand from the fingertip to the principal creases where the finger joins the palm and where the palm joins the wrist.

Prognosis may differ with different types or syndromes. ie. brachydactyly-mesomelia-intellectual disability-heart defects syndrome or if brachydactyly is not isolated and is a part of a larger genetic condition. - Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_2] - Information about: Brachydactyly type D - brachydactyly
Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly type D, also known as murderer's thumb,[3][1] stubbed thumb,[4][5] spoon thumb, power thumb or short thumb,[4][5] is a genetic trait recognised by a thumb being relatively short and round with an accompanying wider nail bed. The distal phalanx of such thumbs is approximately two-thirds the length of full-length thumbs. It is the most common type of shortness of digits (brachydactyly), affecting approximately 2% of the population. It is associated with the HOXD13 gene, located on chromosome 2q31.1.[6]
Section: Signs and symptoms
Brachydactyly type D is a skeletal condition that exhibits a “partial fusion or premature closing of the epiphysis with the distal phalanx of the thumb,” according to Goodman et alia (1965).[5] J.K. Breitenbecher (1923) found that the distal phalanges of short thumbs were one-half the length of full-length thumbs, while R.M. Stecher (1957) claimed that it is approximately two-thirds. The condition may be unilateral (affecting one thumb) or bilateral (affecting both).[5]
Section: Genetics
Brachydactyly type D is a genetic trait. It exhibits autosomal dominance and is commonly developed or inherited independently of other hereditary traits. The condition is associated with the HOXD13 gene, which is central in digital formation and growth.[4] Various other studies supported an autosomal dominant pattern with reduced penetrance.[7][8]
Section: Terminology
The condition is also called clubbed thumb or club thumb.[9][10] American researcher R.A. Hefner used the terms "short thumb" and "brachymegalodactylism" in 1924,[3] and "short thumb" has continued to be used in a few other studies since then, including the study that defined Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome in 1963.[1] "Stub thumb" is the common term preferred by the online database Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man[4] and was first used in a 1965 study.[5] Stub thumbs have also been called hammer thumbs, bohemian thumbs, and potter's thumbs.[4]

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_3] - Information about: Brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome - brachydactyly
Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome is a very rare genetic disorder which is characterized by symmetric brachydactyly of the fingers accompanied by an abnormally long thumb, hypomobility of the shoulder and metacarpo-phalangeal joints, and heart conduction defects. Small feet and hands, small shoulders accompanied with short clavicles, clinodactyly, pectus excavatum, mild limb shortening, cardiomegaly, and pulmonic stenosis murmur have also been reported.[1][2] It was first discovered when D W Hollister et al. described 4 affected members belonging to a 3-generation family.[3][4][5] No new cases have been reported since 1981.[6] This disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.[7]

- Reference: [CRAWL_WIKI_1] - Information about: Brachydactyly
Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly (from Greek  βραχύς (brachus) 'short' and  δάκτυλος (daktulos) 'finger') is a medical term denoting the presence of abnormally short digits (fingers or toes) at birth. The shortness is relative to the length of other long bones and other parts of the body. Brachydactyly is an inherited, dominant trait. It most often occurs as an isolated dysmelia, but can also occur with other anomalies as part of many congenital syndromes. Brachydactyly may also be a signal that one is at risk for congenital heart disease[1] due to the association between congenital heart disease and Carpenter syndrome and the link between Carpenter syndrome and brachydactyly.[2] Nomograms for normal values of finger length as a ratio to other body measurements have been published. In clinical genetics, the most commonly used index of digit length is the dimensionless ratio of the length of the third (middle) finger to the hand length. Both are expressed in the same units (centimeters, for example) and are measured in an open hand from the fingertip to the principal creases where the finger joins the palm and where the palm joins the wrist.
Section: Symptoms
Symptoms of isolated brachydactyly include shorter bones in the hands and feet. This could include, phalanges, metacarpals, metatarsals, carpals, and tarsals. Different types of isolated brachydactyly have different symptoms and they are grouped according to what areas they affect.
Section: Prognosis
Isolated brachydactyly does not affect the wellbeing nor longevity of one's life, in most cases treatment is not necessary.[4] The trait is primarily a cosmetic one and does not, in most cases, affect function of the hands and feet. Even left untreated and affecting function the general diagnosis of brachydactyly does not impact life expectancy. Prognosis may differ with different types or syndromes. ie. brachydactyly-mesomelia-intellectual disability-heart defects syndrome or if brachydactyly is not isolated and is a part of a larger genetic condition. In rare cases of isolated untreated brachydactyly, simple functions like walking or grabbing objects may be difficult, reducing the overall quality of life.

There are several types of brachydactyly:
Section: Other syndromes
In the above brachydactyly syndromes, short digits are the most prominent of the anomalies, but in many other syndromes (Down syndrome, Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome, etc.), brachydactyly is a minor feature compared to the other anomalies or problems comprising the syndrome.

1.question: Which gene is responsible for Carpenter syndrome?

final_answer.long_answer: Carpenter syndrome, formally called acrocephalopolysyndactyly type II, is a rare autosomal-recessive craniosynostosis disorder most often caused by pathogenic variants in RAB23 or MEGF8. Premature fusion of multiple skull sutures produces an acrocephalic (tower-shaped) head, and patients typically show polysyndactyly (extra, fused digits) together with brachydactyly (short fingers and toes). Other frequent manifestations include facial anomalies (flat nasal bridge, low-set or malformed ears), obesity or short stature, congenital heart defects, genital or anal malformations, and varying degrees of developmental delay or intellectual disability.

Small feet and hands, small shoulders accompanied with short clavicles, clinodactyly, pectus excavatum, mild limb shortening, cardiomegaly, and pulmonic stenosis murmur have also been reported.[1][2] It was first discovered when D W Hollister et al. described 4 affected members belonging to a 3-generation family.[3][4][5] No new cases have been reported since 1981.[6] This disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.[7]


- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_2] - Information about: Brachydactyly type D - brachydactyly
Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly type D, also known as murderer's thumb,[3][1] stubbed thumb,[4][5] spoon thumb, power thumb or short thumb,[4][5] is a genetic trait recognised by a thumb being relatively short and round with an accompanying wider nail bed. The distal phalanx of such thumbs is approximately two-thirds the length of full-length thumbs. It is the most common type of shortness of digits (brachydactyly), affecting approximately 2% of the population. It is associated with the HOXD13 gene, located on chromosome 2q31.1.[6]
Section: Signs and symptoms
Brachydactyly type D is a skeletal condition that exhibits a “partial fusion or premature closing of the epiphysis with the distal phalanx of the thumb,” according to Goodman et alia (1965).[5] J.K. Breitenbecher (1923) found that the distal phalanges of short thumbs were one-half the length of full-length thumbs, while R.M. Stecher (1957) claimed that it is approximately two-thirds. The condition may be unilateral (affecting one thumb) or bilateral (affecting both).[5]
Section: Genetics
Brachydactyly type D is a genetic trait. It exhibits autosomal dominance and is commonly developed or inherited independently of other hereditary traits. The condition is associated with the HOXD13 gene, which is central in digital formation and growth.[4] Various other studies supported an autosomal dominant pattern with reduced penetrance.[7][8]
Section: Terminology
The condition is also called clubbed thumb or club thumb.[9][10] American researcher R.A. Hefner used the terms "short thumb" and "brachymegalodactylism" in 1924,[3] and "short thumb" has continued to be used in a few other studies since then, including the study that defined Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome in 1963.[1] "Stub thumb" is the common term preferred by the online database Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man[4] and was first used in a 1965 study.[5] Stub thumbs have also been called hammer thumbs, bohemian thumbs, and potter's thumbs.[4]


- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_1] - Information about: Brachydactyly - brachydactyly
Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly (from Greek  βραχύς (brachus) 'short' and  δάκτυλος (daktulos) 'finger') is a medical term denoting the presence of abnormally short digits (fingers or toes) at birth. The shortness is relative to the length of other long bones and other parts of the body. Brachydactyly is an inherited, dominant trait. It most often occurs as an isolated dysmelia, but can also occur with other anomalies as part of many congenital syndromes. Brachydactyly may also be a signal that one is at risk for congenital heart disease[1] due to the association between congenital heart disease and Carpenter syndrome and the link between Carpenter syndrome and brachydactyly.[2] Nomograms for normal values of finger length as a ratio to other body measurements have been published. In clinical genetics, the most commonly used index of digit length is the dimensionless ratio of the length of the third (middle) finger to the hand length. Both are expressed in the same units (centimeters, for example) and are measured in an open hand from the fingertip to the principal creases where the finger joins the palm and where the palm joins the wrist.
Section: Symptoms
Symptoms of isolated brachydactyly include shorter bones in the hands and feet. This could include, phalanges, metacarpals, metatarsals, carpals, and tarsals. Different types of isolated brachydactyly have different symptoms and they are grouped according to what areas they affect.
Section: Prognosis
Isolated brachydactyly does not affect the wellbeing nor longevity of one's life, in most cases treatment is not necessary.[4] The trait is primarily a cosmetic one and does not, in most cases, affect function of the hands and feet. Even left untreated and affecting function the general diagnosis of brachydactyly does not impact life expectancy. Prognosis may differ with different types or syndromes. ie. brachydactyly-mesomelia-intellectual disability-heart defects syndrome or if brachydactyly is not isolated and is a part of a larger genetic condition. In rare cases of isolated untreated brachydactyly, simple functions like walking or grabbing objects may be difficult, reducing the overall quality of life.

Section: Other syndromes
In the above brachydactyly syndromes, short digits are the most prominent of the anomalies, but in many other syndromes (Down syndrome, Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome, etc.), brachydactyly is a minor feature compared to the other anomalies or problems comprising the syndrome.

Brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome is a very rare genetic disorder which is characterized by symmetric brachydactyly of the fingers accompanied by an abnormally long thumb, hypomobility of the shoulder and metacarpo-phalangeal joints, and heart conduction defects. Small feet and hands, small shoulders accompanied with short clavicles, clinodactyly, pectus excavatum, mild limb shortening, cardiomegaly, and pulmonic stenosis murmur have also been reported.[1][2] It was first discovered when D W Hollister et al. described 4 affected members belonging to a 3-generation family.[3][4][5] No new cases have been reported since 1981.[6] This disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.[7]

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_1] - Information about: Brachydactyly - brachydactyly
Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly (from Greek  βραχύς (brachus) 'short' and  δάκτυλος (daktulos) 'finger') is a medical term denoting the presence of abnormally short digits (fingers or toes) at birth. The shortness is relative to the length of other long bones and other parts of the body. Brachydactyly is an inherited, dominant trait. It most often occurs as an isolated dysmelia, but can also occur with other anomalies as part of many congenital syndromes. Brachydactyly may also be a signal that one is at risk for congenital heart disease[1] due to the association between congenital heart disease and Carpenter syndrome and the link between Carpenter syndrome and brachydactyly.[2] Nomograms for normal values of finger length as a ratio to other body measurements have been published. In clinical genetics, the most commonly used index of digit length is the dimensionless ratio of the length of the third (middle) finger to the hand length. Both are expressed in the same units (centimeters, for example) and are measured in an open hand from the fingertip to the principal creases where the finger joins the palm and where the palm joins the wrist.
Section: Symptoms
Symptoms of isolated brachydactyly include shorter bones in the hands and feet. This could include, phalanges, metacarpals, metatarsals, carpals, and tarsals. Different types of isolated brachydactyly have different symptoms and they are grouped according to what areas they affect.
Section: Prognosis
Isolated brachydactyly does not affect the wellbeing nor longevity of one's life, in most cases treatment is not necessary.[4] The trait is primarily a cosmetic one and does not, in most cases, affect function of the hands and feet. Even left untreated and affecting function the general diagnosis of brachydactyly does not impact life expectancy. Prognosis may differ with different types or syndromes. ie. brachydactyly-mesomelia-intellectual disability-heart defects syndrome or if brachydactyly is not isolated and is a part of a larger genetic condition. In rare cases of isolated untreated brachydactyly, simple functions like walking or grabbing objects may be difficult, reducing the overall quality of life.
Section: Types
There are several types of brachydactyly:
Section: Other syndromes
In the above brachydactyly syndromes, short digits are the most prominent of the anomalies, but in many other syndromes (Down syndrome, Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome, etc.), brachydactyly is a minor feature compared to the other anomalies or problems comprising the syndrome.

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_2] - Information about: Brachydactyly type D - brachydactyly
Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly type D, also known as murderer's thumb,[3][1] stubbed thumb,[4][5] spoon thumb, power thumb or short thumb,[4][5] is a genetic trait recognised by a thumb being relatively short and round with an accompanying wider nail bed. The distal phalanx of such thumbs is approximately two-thirds the length of full-length thumbs. It is the most common type of shortness of digits (brachydactyly), affecting approximately 2% of the population. It is associated with the HOXD13 gene, located on chromosome 2q31.1.[6]
Section: Signs and symptoms
Brachydactyly type D is a skeletal condition that exhibits a “partial fusion or premature closing of the epiphysis with the distal phalanx of the thumb,” according to Goodman et alia (1965).[5] J.K. Breitenbecher (1923) found that the distal phalanges of short thumbs were one-half the length of full-length thumbs, while R.M. Stecher (1957) claimed that it is approximately two-thirds. The condition may be unilateral (affecting one thumb) or bilateral (affecting both).[5]
Section: Genetics
Brachydactyly type D is a genetic trait. It exhibits autosomal dominance and is commonly developed or inherited independently of other hereditary traits. The condition is associated with the HOXD13 gene, which is central in digital formation and growth.[4] Various other studies supported an autosomal dominant pattern with reduced penetrance.[7][8]
Section: Terminology
The condition is also called clubbed thumb or club thumb.[9][10] American researcher R.A. Hefner used the terms "short thumb" and "brachymegalodactylism" in 1924,[3] and "short thumb" has continued to be used in a few other studies since then, including the study that defined Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome in 1963.[1] "Stub thumb" is the common term preferred by the online database Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man[4] and was first used in a 1965 study.[5] Stub thumbs have also been called hammer thumbs, bohemian thumbs, and potter's thumbs.[4]

Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly (from Greek  βραχύς (brachus) 'short' and  δάκτυλος (daktulos) 'finger') is a medical term denoting the presence of abnormally short digits (fingers or toes) at birth. The shortness is relative to the length of other long bones and other parts of the body. Brachydactyly is an inherited, dominant trait. It most often occurs as an isolated dysmelia, but can also occur with other anomalies as part of many congenital syndromes. Brachydactyly may also be a signal that one is at risk for congenital heart disease[1] due to the association between congenital heart disease and Carpenter syndrome and the link between Carpenter syndrome and brachydactyly.[2] Nomograms for normal values of finger length as a ratio to other body measurements have been published. In clinical genetics, the most commonly used index of digit length is the dimensionless ratio of the length of the third (middle) finger to the hand length. Both are expressed in the same units (centimeters, for example) and are measured in an open hand from the fingertip to the principal creases where the finger joins the palm and where the palm joins the wrist.
Section: Symptoms
Symptoms of isolated brachydactyly include shorter bones in the hands and feet. This could include, phalanges, metacarpals, metatarsals, carpals, and tarsals. Different types of isolated brachydactyly have different symptoms and they are grouped according to what areas they affect.
Section: Prognosis
Isolated brachydactyly does not affect the wellbeing nor longevity of one's life, in most cases treatment is not necessary.[4] The trait is primarily a cosmetic one and does not, in most cases, affect function of the hands and feet. Even left untreated and affecting function the general diagnosis of brachydactyly does not impact life expectancy. Prognosis may differ with different types or syndromes. ie. brachydactyly-mesomelia-intellectual disability-heart defects syndrome or if brachydactyly is not isolated and is a part of a larger genetic condition. In rare cases of isolated untreated brachydactyly, simple functions like walking or grabbing objects may be difficult, reducing the overall quality of life.

Section: Introduction
Brachydactyly (from Greek  βραχύς (brachus) 'short' and  δάκτυλος (daktulos) 'finger') is a medical term denoting the presence of abnormally short digits (fingers or toes) at birth. The shortness is relative to the length of other long bones and other parts of the body. Brachydactyly is an inherited, dominant trait. It most often occurs as an isolated dysmelia, but can also occur with other anomalies as part of many congenital syndromes. Brachydactyly may also be a signal that one is at risk for congenital heart disease[1] due to the association between congenital heart disease and Carpenter syndrome and the link between Carpenter syndrome and brachydactyly.[2] Nomograms for normal values of finger length as a ratio to other body measurements have been published. In clinical genetics, the most commonly used index of digit length is the dimensionless ratio of the length of the third (middle) finger to the hand length. Both are expressed in the same units (centimeters, for example) and are measured in an open hand from the fingertip to the principal creases where the finger joins the palm and where the palm joins the wrist.
Section: Symptoms
Symptoms of isolated brachydactyly include shorter bones in the hands and feet. This could include, phalanges, metacarpals, metatarsals, carpals, and tarsals. Different types of isolated brachydactyly have different symptoms and they are grouped according to what areas they affect.

Isolated brachydactyly does not affect the wellbeing nor longevity of one's life, in most cases treatment is not necessary.[4] The trait is primarily a cosmetic one and does not, in most cases, affect function of the hands and feet. Even left untreated and affecting function the general diagnosis of brachydactyly does not impact life expectancy. In rare cases of isolated untreated brachydactyly, simple functions like walking or grabbing objects may be difficult, reducing the overall quality of life.

Small feet and hands, small shoulders accompanied with short clavicles, clinodactyly, pectus excavatum, mild limb shortening, cardiomegaly, and pulmonic stenosis murmur have also been reported.[1][2] It was first discovered when D W Hollister et al. described 4 affected members belonging to a 3-generation family.[3][4][5] No new cases have been reported since 1981.[6] This disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.[7]
